USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the posture just put in place—List 3 at 25 percent, the ICT supply-chain executive order, and the Huawei restriction process—and do not implement List 4 yet. Keep the $300B process running as unused leverage through the June 17 hearing and a possible Trump–Xi window around the G-20, and stay willing to talk without rolling back tariffs or watering down enforcement/IP text. A further tariff blanket now would land on US consumer goods before the May 10 hike and June 1 Chinese retaliation have even fully hit; an immediate concession would reward the walk-back that blew up the endgame.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high. China’s reported late rewrite of already-agreed legal/enforcement language collapsed a near-final deal (May 5–10 timeline; NYT/Politico/Forbes contemporaneous reporting), and Beijing answered the List 3 hike with higher duties on ~$60B of US goods effective June 1, aimed again at agriculture. That hits a politically and economically exposed export sector: soybeans and other farm products were already under 25% Chinese retaliation, 2018 soybean shipments to China were down ~63% Jan–Oct, and Farm Bureau described the new list as hitting farmers at “every single angle,” prompting a proposed ~$15B aid package on top of last year’s $12B. Markets registered the shock—VIX jumped to 20.55 on May 13, 10-year yields fell to 2.37% by May 15, CNY weakened from ~6.73 to 6.87—and List 4 would for the first time tax phones, apparel, toys and other consumer goods. That is why the score is above zero, not a clean opportunity. It is well below +0.5 because the US real economy is still resilient (Michigan sentiment at 100 in May; CPI contained; industrial production only modestly softer), China remains more export-exposed, and US goods imports from China are already down ~15% from December. Action should stay at hold, not another escalate: Washington already raised List 3 on May 10 and signed EO 13873 / moved on Huawei on May 15; USTR has only proposed List 4, with a June 17 hearing, and the President has said he has “not made that decision yet.” Chamber and Business Roundtable are warning that prolonging and broadening tariffs is in neither country’s interest. Immediate List 4 implementation would raise US consumer prices and invite a “fight to the finish” standoff; immediate rollback would forfeit the enforcement mechanism the talks were built around. Hold the new facts on the table, keep talks available, and decide List 4 only after June 1 retaliation and any Beijing/G-20 contact.
key_factors: China walk-back of structural/enforcement text collapsed a near-final deal
List 3 already raised to 25% on May 10; List 4 process open but not implemented
Chinese June 1 retaliation concentrated on US agriculture after prior soybean collapse
US domestic demand still firm (sentiment 100) while markets and CNY show a growth/risk shock
Huawei/ICT EO already opened a non-tariff front on May 15
Further consumer-goods tariffs would shift pain onto US households before last moves have landed

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the already-announced June 1 rate increases on the $60B U.S. list in place, but do not add a new tariff or non-tariff wave in response to the May 15 Huawei move. Invite Lighthizer and Mnuchin back to Beijing and treat a possible late-June G20 meeting as the off-ramp. Hold the line on statutory/enforcement “principle issues” that caused the text rollback; do not offer new purchase or legal-change commitments while List 3 sits at 25% and a further ~$300B list is being prepared.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. The May 10 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% plus USTR’s order to prepare 25% on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese exports reopens a full-coverage shock (timeline 2019-05-05/10; econofact/USTR). That maps onto the CHN +0.5 anchor: major export exposure, FX pressure, Huawei firm-level targeting, and job risk in export hubs. Commerce’s May 15 Entity List action on Huawei and ~70 affiliates, paired with EO 13873, is a qualitative jump from tariffs into a tech choke on China’s national champion (timeline 2019-05-15; Reuters). DEXCHUS weakened from ~6.73 in early May to 6.8742 on May 15; VIX spiked to 20.55 on May 13. AP/PBS cite ~0.5pp of Chinese growth at risk from the latest U.S. duties and up to ~1pp if both sides cover remaining trade, enough to push growth toward/below 6% and raise politically dangerous unemployment. Coastal plants have already seen sharp U.S.-bound order drops. This is not +1.0: industrial production is still +5.0% YoY, merchandise exports remain firm on a SA basis (~$211B in May), and reserves are stable near $3.12T.

Action should stay near zero, not escalate. China already matched the List 3 hike by raising rates on its existing ~$60B U.S. list (5–25%, June 1). Further escalation—rare earths, ag embargo, Treasury talk, or a Huawei-style hit on U.S. firms—would give Washington a pretext to finalize the remaining ~$300B list, which China cannot symmetrically tariff because of the lopsided goods balance. Liu He said talks have not broken down and China will not concede on principle issues; the ambassador has invited U.S. principals to Beijing and a Trump–Xi G20 contact is still live. That is the correct band: negotiate without new commitments. Conceding purchases or writing U.S. demands into Chinese law now would reward a mid-talks tariff hike and a national-champion blacklist. Holding fire on a second wave while keeping the channel open preserves optionality and avoids turning a costly trade fight into an immediate tech-and-growth crisis.
key_factors: List 3 raised to 25% on ~$200B (May 10) with USTR preparing 25% on remaining ~$300B
Huawei + ~70 affiliates moved toward Entity List / EO 13873 on May 15 — firm-level tech choke
Talks broke over China deleting legal-change commitments (IP, tech transfer, competition, financial services, currency); Liu He: talks not dead, no concession on principle issues
CNY weakened ~6.73 to 6.87 in early May; VIX spike; ~0.5–1pp GDP-at-risk estimates; coastal export-order stress
China already scheduled June 1 retaliation on $60B and is short of further U.S. goods to tariff; G20/Beijing channel still open
